SCF #46 / DEVELOPER TOOLING / OPEN TRACK

Stellar Discovery
Trust Layer

From an approved payment
to complete, useful work.

TokenJunkieLabs requests USD 38,000 equivalent in XLM for 400 prospective delivery hours over 150 days from actual award acceptance. The work installs a useful paid Stellar service with two independently operated merchants, two independent buyer operators and the same selected operation through two independently operated facilitators.

The product is open-source, self-hostable merchant and buyer tooling. It carries an approved API request, dataset or paid MCP tool through native settlement, complete useful output, fulfillment and operating handover. The merchant controls its source and terms. The buyer controls its keys, request and spending. Another engineer can reopen the installation and recover unfinished work.

The working development baseline comprises 18 distinct team-operated purchases totaling 411,000 stroops, or 0.0411 native testnet XLM, with network fees recorded separately. The funded milestones establish independent customer operation, repeated use and production receiving from that baseline.

Project and requested outcome

TokenJunkieLabs is building Stellar Discovery Trust Layer, open-source, self-hostable merchant and buyer software for selling a useful API, dataset or agent operation on Stellar. It connects the approved request, native payment, complete customer output and merchant fulfillment in one continuing operation.

We request $38,000 for 400 prospective delivery hours over 150 days from award acceptance, under SCF #46 Build / Open Track. The grant will adapt and install the existing product with two independently operated merchants, establish use by at least two independent buyer operators, and leave each installation with another engineer who can run, change and recover it. By day 90, the same useful service will operate through two independently operated testnet facilitators. By day 150, both merchant installations will operate on mainnet with repeat independent use.

The first deployment is a recurring API/data task: a merchant publishes an authorized report, dataset or query; the buyer approves its scope and price; and the complete result enters the buyer's actual application. A source update supplies a new useful edition. If delivery is interrupted after settlement, the customer continues the original purchase and receives its unfinished output.

The starting product already implements payment, retained requests, source-aware receiving and recovery. The award funds the remaining reusable Stellar integration, customer-source adaptations, independent deployment, monitoring and production handover required by the selected services. Completed pre-award work is reconciled out of the remaining estimate before the grant work is assigned.

Customer problem, need and adoption

Our first customer is a recurring API/data-service operator, or the implementation agency bringing that service into a customer's application. Two commercial roles must be clear: the commissioning payer funds the installation and handover; the independent buyer pays the merchant for a useful resource. A platform may introduce the customer while the agency contracts for the integration. Those responsibilities are agreed in the original workorder.

The practical problem appears after a payment succeeds. An analyst still needs every agreed page, correct units and time basis, and a report they can edit. An agent needs the approved result within the whole task's spending limit. A merchant needs to know which order was fulfilled. The next engineer must be able to reopen the customer state and finish an interrupted delivery. A response, a transfer and a completed customer task are separate events that the application connects.

A concrete first use case is a recurring environmental or economic briefing. The customer selects its source, geography or other population, observation period and expected report. The merchant reviews and releases that edition. The buyer acquires the advertised HTML, CSV, JSON or named query result and receives it in its existing analyst workspace. The priced unit is exactly the advertised resource: if the agreed task needs several paid pages or separately priced files, its workorder and buyer approval account for their combined cost and complete coverage. A later source period or distinct useful query creates the next purchase.

Our maintained product has already taken a complete 140-observation, six-sensor air-quality study into a separately reopened customer project, and received a 144-row municipal selection through two paid pages with both transfers and the combined dataset retained. These operated tasks make the proposed customer installation and handover concrete. The Timescale use case applies the same receiving requirement to original reports and native sources, explicit field/time/quality interpretation, baseline-to-observed accounting and an analytical workspace another engineer can continue.

The selection records the actual recurring task, authorized source, expected complete output, priced unit, buyer spending limit, merchant host, receiving engineer and acceptance owner. A funding assignment then places each remaining adaptation once in a grant package or a separately commissioned workorder.

Adoption follows that same installed workflow. The merchant publishes the agreed service; an independent buyer receives and accepts its output; a later source edition or useful query supplies repeat use; and another engineer performs an actual change or recovery. We will compare the customer's previous method with the installed task on the same source scope: active effort, manual corrections and time to accepted output.

The purchase target has a customer calendar. Thirty purchases over fourteen consecutive days require thirty distinct useful paid requests. Two buyers making one purchase on each ordinary weekday generate only twenty over that window. Before selecting the T3 calendar, the workorders therefore establish actual demand for thirty purchases: for example, three independent weekday users across the two merchants, or a documented mix of recurring reports and additional useful queries by at least two buyers. Two independent buyers remain the acceptance minimum. Reopening a saved result, retrying its original request or subdividing an unchanged task does not manufacture repeat adoption.

TokenJunkieLabs sells defined implementation and separately scoped care. Merchants retain their resource proceeds; implementation partners retain their customer relationships. Accepted scope, actual delivery effort, corrections, collections and support load inform the next installation's price.

An aid-data publisher or its implementation partner needs the original organisation publication, selected activity portfolios and reviewed financial result to remain usable together. The analyst selects the actual reporting period and coverage, retains the original currencies and dates, reviews findings and receives the complete editable work. The existing AidStream offer prices an organisation publication and receiving installation at USD 6,400 over ten business days; the complete IATI chapter connects that commissioning model to the merged financial-review product.

Why Stellar and what we contribute

Stellar provides the native authorization and settlement for the reviewed purchase. In the x402 Exact Stellar flow, the buyer signs a Soroban authorization entry identifying the payer, recipient, atomic token amount and expiration. The selected facilitator verifies and submits the authorization under its network and fee policy. Sponsored settlement lets the buyer use a supported payment token while the facilitator pays the transaction fee.

We compose the existing Stellar SDKs, wallets, token contracts and x402 payment services. The ledger records the transfer. Private merchant and buyer workspaces retain the approved HTTP method or MCP tool and arguments, source selection, spending decision, complete result and fulfillment history. The original transaction and request identities connect those records through interruption and receiving.

The ecosystem already supplies substantial payment, discovery and access tooling. The Stellar x402 CLI guide demonstrates the challenge, signed retry, returned response and transfer confirmation, and explains why saving the returned body matters when another request incurs another payment. x402 facilitators provide verification and settlement; Bazaar publishes discoverable resource schemas.

Existing solutionPublished capability and our implementation focus
ApiChargeSigned route quotes and time-bound access grants, with call/data/credit limits and Soroban settlement. Our funded work carries the acquired resource into a complete editable customer application and operating handover.
NiriumTypeScript/Python payment SDKs, seller middleware, MCP and CLI. Our customer installation joins approved intent, original attempts, settled result, complete output and recovery in its retained merchant/buyer state.
MPP RouterDiscovery, agent-wallet connection and paid service calls using Stellar USDC. Our selected customer task keeps its complete multi-page or file coverage, analytical output and later source edition.
Stellar RavenMCP access to Stellar documentation and ecosystem operations. Our merchant publishes its own priced resource and hands that complete customer service to a receiving maintainer.

Our contribution is complete paid-work receiving and continued operation: task-level approval and aggregate cost, source-faithful results, durable unfinished-delivery recovery, recurring useful editions, and merchant/accounting handover. The completed municipal example combines two purchases into one 144-row customer task and reopens its CSV/JSONL with source and accounting. The paid-query example preserves the actual limited result and its truncation status in another receiving directory. Browser, CLI, typed-client and MCP interfaces continue the original saved state.

The grant uses Open Track for these reusable merchant-and-buyer capabilities. The six packages apply the existing architecture to the selected independent services and return the deployment, source/receiving, monitoring and recovery improvements to the public product.

Deployment is network-specific. The Stellar x402 documentation identifies hosted Vellar as testnet-only. A retained catalogue comparison found 27 Vellar offers and two Periplo offers with no shared seller/route identity, so T2 explicitly funds registration and payment-policy compatibility for the same useful service across two independent facilitators. T3 uses each merchant's reviewed mainnet-capable configuration. The native signer and facilitator source already supports explicit networks, allowed assets and recipients, fee ceilings, separate signing accounts and admission/drain controls.

Defined architecture and operating behavior

The implementation has six cooperating components: a private merchant source/release workspace; its public HTTP or MCP service; the native Stellar signer and facilitator; private buyer approval and spending state; complete delivery records and received output; and merchant fulfillment/accounting.

StageOperating behavior and retained state
Select and publishThe merchant chooses an authorized source edition or named live query, schema, complete output and limits. Review fixes the route, network, asset, recipient, amount and authorization lifetime. A later source or terms change becomes a separately reviewed edition.
Connect the sourceAdapters preserve types, nulls, keys, pagination, units, time basis and snapshot/live behavior. Customer-controlled credential or OAuth references select access. The returned result identifies its source edition.
Approve and payThe buyer retains the HTTP method or MCP endpoint, tool and arguments, request-body identity, task scope and accepted payment option. The remote schema and full payment challenge must match before signing. Per-payment limits and the existing reservation/budget owner govern aggregate task spending.
Settle and receiveThe facilitator verifies and settles the native authorization. Independent RPC reconciliation checks network, asset, parties and atomic amount. The application retains the complete result, merchant notification and receiving acknowledgment. A multi-request task keeps its total cost and unfinished coverage.
Use and accountThe customer opens the selected pages and files in its actual application. Merchant pricing binds its tariff and saved quote to an observed usage period, counting basis and supplier-cost basis. Reviewed repricing carries that source into the customer quotation and original invoice or service records.
Recover and hand overServer confirmation, observed transfer, output and fulfillment remain individually readable. An uncertain signed response continues through its original dispatch. A receiving engineer restores configuration, history and customer files, supplies existing secret references and completes the original operation.

A saved prepaid call retains its selected pass when another becomes the default. Replaying the original completed request retains its result and consumed allowance. A replacement pass links to its predecessor and keeps previously acquired results available. Additional advertised requests retain their own terms and spending decisions.

Node.js supplies the merchant, buyer, browser, CLI, typed-client and MCP interfaces; paid MCP uses the official SDK for payment and settlement metadata. Python and SQLite retain typed data and saved analytical queries; PHP provides the native WordPress/WooCommerce integration. Source and receiving applications keep their native semantics. The six-package request uses existing SDKs and token contracts. The proposed architecture and source are defined before award; the funded implementation connects them to the selected customers' actual routes, sources, hosts and operating arrangements.

At selection, each customer workorder names its current source and operating gap, remaining adaptation, original package, implementation output and acceptance owner. As reusable improvements finish before award, their completed work is removed from the remaining request through the existing package model. A separately commissioned installation receives its own commercial allocation. Every remaining activity is charged once. If a Timescale installation is selected, its work connects the actual customer source/host, reviewed complete resource, approved buyer request and original receiving application; repeat use, provider attribution, deployed recovery and engineer handover belong to the same six packages.

The usage targets include no purchase subsidy. Existing implementation, general operations, sales, purchase principal and network fees have separate funding. Existing compute is the starting resource; incremental service reserve and hosted Actions budget are $0. Each workorder names the actual host and the party responsible for service charges and purchases.

If an IATI publisher installation is selected, its remaining work connects the actual organisation and activity editions, reviewed financial resource, approved buyer purchase and complete report/package to the existing merchant and receiving application. Customer adaptation, independent provider deployment, recurring use, recovery and receiving-engineer handover remain within the six funded packages.

Threat response and outcome measurement

T2's 50-hour / $4,750 response package delivers the installed threat model and monitoring procedure. Each merchant/buyer installation records the source edition, authority, network and facilitator; protected state and observation sources; reviewed thresholds and notification destinations; and named primary and backup responders.

The threat model covers changed offers or approvals, incorrect payment/output attribution, unauthorized access, interrupted delivery, missing observations and restoration of the wrong generation. The installed customer operates two response cases: an interrupted settled purchase and a merchant-delivery failure. Each retains notification and acknowledgment, financial and delivery state, response/recovery times, correction and the receiving engineer's reopening. A monitoring interruption remains visible while observation is recovered.

The cohort measures useful customer work using the following definitions:

MeasureCounting and acceptance
Completed purchaseOne distinct approved intent, independently observed native transfer and complete useful output. Deduplicate the transaction within its network; keep asset amounts and fees separate.
Prepaid purchaseCount the settled pass once when its first agreed operation has complete accepted output. Later allowance calls are usage. A replacement requires its own settlement and first useful completion to count as another purchase.
Complete customer taskReceive and accept every agreed page, file or application result. Preserve total cost, completed coverage and unfinished work beside the individually priced requests.
Independent and returning buyersCount the accountable organization/person across its wallets and agents. Both merchants receive independent use. A returning buyer completes a distinct qualifying purchase on another UTC day.
Two facilitatorsComplete the same useful service, schema, source population and output through each independent operator, retaining actual payment terms and results.
Recovery and handoverContinue the original request and financial outcome, reopen selected files/history, reconcile later operations and complete the maintainer's support case.

The acceptance windows are ten useful purchases in total across the buyer cohort in T2's seven days, and thirty in total in T3's fourteen days, with at least two independent buyers and both merchants represented. The deployment calendar records the actual recurring reports and useful queries expected to supply those purchases. Additional buyer operators may participate; their identity and useful task remain explicit.

The Queens HPD example illustrates the distinction: two paid pages and two transfers totaling 20,000 native testnet stroops deliver one complete 144-row customer task. The eight-unit pass illustrates another: its 10,000-stroop purchase counts once with the first useful operation, while two consumed and six remaining units describe usage. Reopening either result retains its original task.

The seven- and fourteen-day cohorts retain all attempted, completed, partial, unresolved, canceled and refunded outcomes. Original first-attempt time determines purchase-window membership; native settlement, complete accepted output and any applicable order completion must occur within that same window. The observation cutoff can retain later observations without moving a later completion into the earlier window. The reviewed customer/operator declarations establish independence; team activity retains its own baseline.

For each selected task, compare the prior method, first installed use and later recurring use on the same source population or period and expected output: active effort, manual corrections, time to useful output, acceptance and unresolved work. Pricing retains quantity, counting basis, period and supplier-cost coverage. Commercial measurement follows agreed scope, accepted milestones, issued fees, actual collections and support effort in the original workorder and accounting records.

For a stated evaluation period, direct labor value is completed tasks multiplied by active hours saved per comparable task and the customer's stated hourly value, less the one-time implementation fee and total incremental provider, hosting, payment and support costs during that period. Record those inputs with the original workorder; the same calculation gives the effort reduction needed to recover the fee. Compare the initial result, the following source period and an independent maintainer's change or recovery.

Delivery capacity, payment timing and sustainability

Bryce is accountable for allocating contributors and operating resources to the six packages. The retained resource study allocates 400 hours over 150 days. Its lowest examined timely allocation is 25 engineering hours plus eight integration/handover hours per week. This is a modeled allocation; named contributor availability and payment arrangements are being finalized against the actual award date.

SCF's four payments would be $3,800 at award acceptance, then $7,600, $11,400 and $15,200 after the respective deliverables are approved. Those cash receipts differ from the tranche delivery costs of $11,400 / $11,400 / $15,200. Under the Official Rules, the USD-equivalent award is paid in XLM using CF XLMUSD_RR, or SDF's selected qualifying alternative, on the actual payment day.

Working capital is part of the delivery plan. With the retained labor-accrual assumptions, peak additional cash is $17,250 with a 14-day review/payment lag, $23,275 with 30 days, and $26,600 with 60 days. Opening cash and a committed bridge or contributor deferral have not been entered. Actual available funds, collections and agreed contributor payment timing must cover the modeled requirement before the corresponding dated delivery commitments are made.

Grant and accepted commercial work share one contributor capacity plan. A commercial workshare adds its actual hours, dependencies and acceptance dates, with available capacity allocated once. Bryce reconciles the combined schedule and expected collections before agreeing dated work, using separately named capacity or an agreed timing change.

Each tranche completion form is due within 90 calendar days of the preceding payment. If a delay is anticipated, the operator seeks SDF's written acknowledgment before the original deadline and uses a revised deadline only when confirmed in writing.

Sustainability comes from reusable open-source deployment and receiving capabilities, paid customer-specific implementation and separately scoped care. Each installation retains estimated and actual effort, included corrections, support responsibility, acceptance and collections. A support engagement starts from the customer's installed state and recovery procedure. Measured adaptation and care effort inform following offers, while completed pre-award source is removed from the prospective grant estimate.
